Forget b, new_nonce and tmp_aes data after dh_gen_ok
note: Fixed 2026-10-07 (security-row pass). Before: Byte buffers are zeroized, also on errors; new_nonce is zeroized best effort (moves between states copy it); the BigUint exponent is only dropped. A scanning allocator finds new_nonce (stale bytes the state moves leave behind), the key (to_fixed_be's Vec), b and g_a^b (num-bigint and its modpow intermediates) in freed memory (ignored tests); tmp_aes data stays on the stack and is wiped.

requirement: Initial salt = new_nonce[0..8] ⊕ server_nonce[0..8]
A stalled handshake has a deadline and is retried on another connection
Plain envelope: auth_key_id = 0, bounded length, never panics
note: The server msg_id of plain messages is not checked (tdlib checks parity).

requirement: A partial frame that averages under 512 B/s after a 15 s grace is abandoned; slow links above that are never cut
note: With the 4 MiB cap a fake frame trickled at the floor holds a session at most about 2.3 h. 2026-10-06: the grace is given once per fresh packet, matched quick ack or handshake step, so empty frames cannot hold a dead connection.

requirement: Debug output never prints proxy secrets or session verification tokens
Obfuscation keys, proxy secrets (ProxySecret, DcAddress, ProxyConfig, SOCKS5 password) and secret FFI payloads dropped after shutdown are zeroized
note: Checked with a scanning allocator on the test and engine threads. The named types wipe themselves, but copies do not (ignored tests): Socks5Auth and the SOCKS5 request in the write buffer, the fake-TLS key in TlsState, HTTP Basic credentials, and a partly decoded standard-base64 secret. requirement: RSA public keys from PEM/DER never panic; only 2048-bit moduli with an odd exponent of at least 3 are accepted
note: Also fuzzed by the rsa target. The exponent check is new.

requirement: No attacker-reachable panic in packet, handshake or transport parsing
HTTP: transport errors arrive as HTTP status codes and the body is ignored
note: Error bodies are discarded up to 64 KiB.

requirement: HTTP: a 404 or a 2xx page from a captive portal or proxy must not count as a lost auth key or a delivered answer, and the route check itself must neither stall nor storm
note: A 404 counts only right after a plain req_pq on the route came back with the server's res_pq; any other answer to the check backs off like a refused route, and so does an error status on a handshake request. A 2xx answer that is not a packet under the session's key (a portal page, an empty body) is never taken for a delivered response: the request counts as lost and the route is checked, backing off.

requirement: HTTP responses from a hostile server or middlebox are bounded (head, headers, body, chunks, time) and never confuse framing (Content-Length vs Transfer-Encoding)
note: Fuzz target `http` (300 000 cases). A head (or endless 1xx) trickled byte by byte is cut a response timeout + 15 s after its first byte.

requirement: Under engine PFS nothing but the bind goes out under an unbound temporary key, even when a salt failure or a reconnect re-queues the bind behind other queries
Replacing a temporary key never runs a query twice: requests the server may already have are not moved to the new session
note: They fail to the host as 500 TEMP_KEY_ROTATED when the key has to go while they are unanswered, and so do requests chained after them with invoke_after. The new key starts on fresh connections (as tdlib closes its connections), so the old session's late packets never meet the new handshake. Requests carry what the client knew about them (open retry questions, FLOOD_WAIT, verifications) into the new session. Events the old client still held for the host are delivered; requests queued between clients get the same size check as at send. The same holds when the host clears or replaces the key under PFS. A key the server loses (-404, e.g. a restart dropping temporary keys) is not a replacement the engine chose: calls in flight then go again under the new key, as without PFS and in tdlib; the API's random_id makes the non-idempotent ones safe. Accepted exception (2026-10-06, audit B-3): forged -404 frames under engine PFS move in-flight requests to the new temporary key session; the host would resubmit them after a rotation anyway (MtProtoKit and tdlib behave the same).

requirement: destroy_auth_key must destroy the permanent key, not a temporary key bound to it
note: As tdlib's destroying session (Session.cpp: need_destroy_auth_key turns PFS off and sends no queries): destroy_auth_key goes under the permanent key on fresh connections while every request waits; once answered, the requests go under a new permanent key and temporary key. A pending destroy keeps an idle session connected. A destroy lost with its connection or HTTP request goes again until answered (tdlib sends it on every new connection); it belongs to the key it was asked for and never goes under a replacement. Without PFS too, no call goes while destroy_auth_key is unanswered (tdlib: need_send_query is false while destroying); enable_pfs during a destroy finishes the destroy before any key is made.

requirement: A server refusing every bind must not make the engine run key handshakes back to back
note: A refused key is replaced at once the first time, then after 1 s doubling to 60 s until a key is bound. A pending bind keeps the link, without waking the worker. Over HTTP each handshake step may take another connection, as on a route without keep-alive. The backoff holds across permanent keys the host hands over until a key is bound, so a host answering every PermanentKeyInvalid with a new key does not churn connections.

requirement: After the host hands over another permanent key no call runs under a temporary key bound to the old one
note: The temporary key goes at once; calls in flight fail as TEMP_KEY_ROTATED.

requirement: HTTP: a datacenter address or proxy given by host name is resolved and cached like the TCP transport's
note: Lookups go through a per-session cache (host:port, TTL 299 s); a TCP retry waits only for its own lookup. A name that does not resolve is looked up again with the TCP transport's backoff (a short negative cache); consecutive failures rotate through a name's addresses. Each name keeps the address that works: the HTTP transport moves past an address only when that address failed, so later connections never go back to a dead one; only lookups for hosts it connects to count against it. Each name remembers which of its addresses failed (a connect error, or no answer with requests cut); the next connection takes the first one that has not, or the one that failed longest ago; an answer clears it. A finished lookup wakes HTTP and the Auto probe instead of polling.

requirement: HTTP connection attempts back off like the TCP transport's: cut connections, the offline probe interval, proxy refusals, and a fresh start on network or proxy changes
note: The open backoff resets only once the server answered; connections cut with requests in flight back off like flapping stream connections (0.5 s doubling to 16 s). A session that wants no link closes HTTP even with no connection left, so it never waits on a link it does not have; failed key creations back off as over TCP; unreachable proxies and refusals after a proxy change are reported. A handshake held between steps is dropped when the session wants no link; a session reset that waits for old answers (bad_msg 17) goes out as soon as it is due. Seeded session explorer (session_explorer_tests.rs) checks no spin, no stall, no duplicate, no panic over random host commands and faults. Auto opens no HTTP probe while the current TCP connection answers, whatever failed before it.

requirement: HTTP: a session reset after bad_msg_notification 17 must not run calls twice: it waits for every answer the old session may still get, and keeps receiving them
note: While the reset drains, long polls stay parked under the old session, and queries whose request was lost but may have reached the server are waited for like sent ones. Requests go first to connections that answered, and long polls on connections that never answered do not count toward the parked ones once one has, so old answers have a way back.

requirement: TCP: a datacenter address or proxy given by host name keeps trying the address that answered after a drop instead of going back to a dead first address, and a racer never races the primary's own address
note: Before: the cached addresses were read from the failure count, which an answer clears, so every attempt after a drop went to the first address again (27 connections to a black hole, 148 s for the next call). The answering address now leads the cached list and a new lookup of the name; a racer for a name with one address entry takes the name's next resolved address.

requirement: An answer held up longer than the 300 s time window (an outage) still completes the query it answers, instead of leaving it waiting for ever
note: A packet outside the time window is taken when it carries the rpc_result of a query the session still waits for (only the server's own answer can match); its time does not reset the server clock, nor does the old answer's own msg_id, even inside a fresh container or with the clock running ahead when the query went out, and a pong in it is no round-trip sample. Other old packets are still ignored. Such a packet is taken as a replay: only results, pongs, state info, salts and updates act, so nothing else in it (a bad_msg_notification, new_session_created) can move the clock or the session; it is taken even below the received-message floor. Each pass over such a packet (freshness proof, awaited answer, processing) has its own unpack budget; only the server's own packets get that far.

requirement: Transport frames, quick acks and empty frames are unauthenticated: they are hints, never proof (an on-path box can forge -404/-429/-444)
The fake-TLS ServerHello is bound to this ClientHello (HMAC over client_random)
Only fresh packets prove a connection answered (address success, racer, rejection counters)
Replays of packets evicted from the duplicate window never drive liveness, stuck detection or dropped-answer accounting
One difference fetch per new update loss: a replayed evicted update packet cannot storm UpdatesLost
A rejected container re-asks for future salts at once instead of holding every query for 60 s
Non-finite time inputs from the host are ignored
Host wrapper inputs TL cannot carry (≥16 MiB strings, unaligned init params) fail the request locally instead of aborting
Host request ids in the reserved bind id range are refused; the bind still works
C ABI robustness: null/dangling inputs, unknown handles, re-entrant callbacks, no events after destroy, many threads, destroy from a callback
Logs carry no keys, salts, secrets or message bodies; created keys are never printed by Debug
Injected or forged transport frames never touch the key, clock or salts; forged errors during key creation back off; forged quick acks are cheap
Route memory from storage is bounded and never panics
Handshake answers recorded from an earlier exchange are refused at every step; a reflected client packet is refused; a forged plain packet changes nothing in an established session
A CDN session never reports its clock to the host
A CDN cannot start an APNs/reCAPTCHA verification: such requests fail the call
